title: cairn new makes an app that links
text: Since the library split, the Cairn umbrella imported every proof and tool, none of which an app links, so an app that wrote import Cairn, as cairn new's template did, failed at the host's link on initialize_cairn_Cairn (#128). Now Cairn is the linked library's umbrella, with the claim commands at compile time only, and the everything-umbrella the ledger, the audit and the docs read is CairnAll. cairn new --bin writes a working app: a place, a move, its exports, the C declaration of its initializer and a host with a selftest. make check now builds one against the checkout, runs its selftest and locks its two claims, which takes about a minute.

title: Gallery: images
caption: Six image tiles, each a 200 × 150 Node.image that Lean lays out before any pixels exist: a PNG, a JPEG turned by its EXIF orientation, a GIF, a poster over https, a text file and a missing file. The host decodes with ImageIO and paints with Metal; Lean only learns the pixel size, or the fault, from the loadImage reply. Reload (^501) sends every tile back to its grey placeholder and reads each source again; Fit (^502) cycles cover, contain and stretch. Nothing moves when a picture arrives or fails. In the self test every tile was answered 6.8 ms after launch.

title: cairn_json, the first package outside the cairn repository
text: Yap's JSON parser and encoder is now its own registry package, cairn_json 0.1.0, in iamnbutler/cairn_json. It requires cairn ^0.1.2 from the registry, is pure Lean with no Swift and no extern, and leaves Yap's date arithmetic for a later cairn_date.

The library is 491 lines. 793 lines of proofs hold 49 theorems: decode (encode v) = some v and decode (pretty v) = some v for every value nested at most 512 deep, and that more fuel never changes what the parser answers. decode is total by construction, with no partial def. The axiom audit allows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and the kernel replays every declaration.

A trusted fuzz check compares it with Foundation's JSONSerialization: 220,164 documents per seed (valid, mutated, UTF-16 and UTF-32, random bytes and 164 edge cases), 5 seeds, 0 unexplained differences. The known ones are listed in its docs/trusted.md: numbers Foundation can't hold, a leading U+FEFF Foundation drops from strings, short UTF-16 and UTF-32 documents without a byte order mark, invalid UTF-8, and nesting 513 deep.
The commit is cairn_json's.

title: cairn-link links each dependency's libraries
text: bin/cairn-link no longer links Cairn's library by name (#118). It reads lake-manifest.json, finds the cairn.toml beside each dependency, transitive ones included, and links the Lean libraries that package lists under libs. Cairn's own cairn.toml now lists Cairn, so an app gets the same archive as before, and a library like cairn_json can be linked the same way.

It refuses a Lean module that ends up in two archives, which would be a duplicate symbol, and a dependency that is an app. A dependency with no cairn.toml is linked not at all; if linked code imports it, cairn-link names the package and says to give it one.

Checked with a throwaway app that depends on Cairn and on a second library package with its own libs: it links, and a small C program draws a frame through both. Yap builds against it with its existing --lib Yap and passes its selftest.

title: Cairn 0.1.3, on the public registry
text: Cairn 0.1.3 is out, and it is on the public registry at cairn.registry.nexthub.sh as iamnbutler/cairn, next to 0.1.2. Reading it needs no login: cairn add cairn finds the owner by name and writes the version range, and Lake fetches Cairn from the registry's git (#107, #109). /packages/ now reads the registry itself instead of sample data (#111).

The Cairn library is now only what an app links: 31 modules. Proofs, claims, fuzzing and tools are their own Lake libraries, so libcairn_Cairn.a went from 3.67 to 2.78 MB (#114). Three modules moved so the directories in lean/ have no cycles, and make lint now fails on one; the old names stay as shims until 0.2.0 (#110).
No claim changed, so it is a patch release. Yap moved to it with only its tag changed.

title: Cairn 0.1.2: libraries and apps
text: Cairn 0.1.2 is out. A package is now a library or an app, as in Cargo: cairn.toml has kind = "lib" or "bin", cairn new asks which, and /packages/ lists apps under their own tab (#103). Nothing can depend on an app.
cairn publish sends no docs. HTML from a publisher would run as the registry's site, so docs will be built from the source instead, as docs.rs does (#98).
The ledger now treats retiring a released claim as a breaking change: it needs a new major version, or a new minor one while at 0.x (#100). No claim changed in 0.1.2, so it is a patch release.

title: Cairn is a package, and Yap moved out
text: Cairn is now a package. An app lives in its own repository and depends on a tagged release, and one tag pins both halves: the Lean package and the Swift libraries. v0.1.0 is the first release (#80). v0.1.1 fixes cairn doc, which failed in apps because it read its stylesheet from the app (#91).
Yap moved out first. It lives in its own repository, yap-cairn, and depends on Cairn v0.1.0 like any other app would. Its Lean, proofs, fuzzers, Swift host and benches left this repository with it.

Claim ids are now scoped by package. Cairn's are cairn^N and Yap's are yap^N, so “a shortcut never sends” is yap^311. Cairn's claims.lock still lists Yap's old ids, marked moved:yap, so they can never be issued here again.

title: The cairn command and packages
text: There is now a cairn command (#79). cairn new starts a package in its own repository with its claim scope set, cairn add depends on another package, and cairn build runs Lake, links the Lean into one library and builds the Swift host. cairn doc writes the package's docs, and cairn publish and cairn login talk to a registry. It has unit tests, and it has been run against a stand-in registry but not a deployed one yet.

The registry is nextpm, a package registry, with a new cairn kind (nextpm #22). It has an index Lake reads natively, the source served over git, and a build cache, so that lake cache get downloads prebuilt Lean. Its claim ledger refuses a version that drops, renumbers or redefines an id. /packages/ shows a registry's packages, and until one is running it shows sample data (#78).
Publishers no longer upload docs. A registry now refuses HTML from a publisher (nextpm #23), and docs will be built from the source by a builder we run, the way docs.rs works (#94).

title: Developer docs and the API reference
text: Developer docs are up at /docs, laid out like Rust's bookshelf: the Cairn Book, Cairn by Example, reference pages, and guides to working on Cairn itself (#76). Every code sample is included from a source file that make check compiles, so a sample can't drift from the code it shows. Moving an included region fails the build until the page is fixed.

The API reference at /docs/api/ is generated by cairn doc, Cairn's answer to rustdoc (#77). It reads the Lean environment directly instead of using doc-gen4. On TodoMVC, doc-gen4 took 185 s and wrote 227 MB, almost all of it Lean's own library. Each claim appears on its module's page with its statement, evidence and proofs. A Lean block in a doc comment is a doc test that make check runs.
Every heading on the site also has an id now, and a # that copies a link to it (#72).

title: Yap against the original under Instruments
text: Yap on Cairn was measured against the original Yap with Apple's Instruments rather than Cairn's own tools (#65). At 60 Hz the two overlays now pace the same, at 59.3 and 59.9 frames a second, with no hitches in either.

While recording, Cairn used 205 ms of CPU a second, against the original's 82. Most of that went to redrawing the menu bar's status item on every frame. Once its properties were written only when they change, an A/B run went from 197 to 98 ms/s.

The overlay now appears only once the microphone is running, as in the original, so a microphone that fails no longer flashes it (#68, yap^349). On a 120 Hz display, Cairn drew 118 frames a second where the original draws 60. It's now capped at 60, and it checks files every 2 s, as the original does (#69). The idle runs and a check on a 60 Hz display are still to do (#70).

title: Yap on Cairn: the overlay
caption: Yap's dictation overlay on Cairn, driven by a synthetic voice: recording with a moving tape waveform and a two-line live preview, then transcribing, then typed. The state, view and layout are Lean; the waveform is a host-drawn paint node running the original's Metal shader.

title: Clock: effects
caption: Cairn's first effects. A stopwatch whose time, ticks, sounds and lap file come from the host as replies to requests Lean makes: Lap plays a sound, Save writes the laps to a file, Reset clears them and Load reads them back. Timers fire within 1–2 ms; a click → read file → frame round trip is 1.5 ms (p50).

title: TodoMVC in Lean
caption: The full TodoMVC, written in Lean and running natively on the Mac. Add, complete, double-click to edit, filter, clear completed, and toggle all. Every control is a claim (^202 to ^211). On the real app, 999 of 1,000 generated conformance sequences matched the Lean model. The one miss is a known edge case: a click that ends an edit can be dropped, as in a browser.

title: Basics: the first Lean app
caption: A whole app written in Lean: adding, ticking and deleting items. Lean decides the layout, focus, text editing and hit testing; Swift only draws. Every control is a claim (^101 to ^104). Lean proves that an item's Delete button exists exactly when the item does, and that the 'items left' count is right.

title: The host, with text
caption: The new AppKit host painting through the Metal renderer: Core Text glyphs from an atlas, a caret, a focused field, a checkbox and a list. Typing goes through the Mac's text-input path, and every control in the accessibility tree is named by its claim id (^1 field, ^2 checkbox, ^3 Add, ^4#1 the new item). This app is the host's test fixture, with its frames built in Swift; the next video is the same host running a Lean app.

title: Boundary spike
caption: The first thing on screen. Lean owns the state, the layout and the hit test; Swift forwards clicks and paints Lean's rectangles with Metal. The bar is the count (no text rendering yet). Reset (red) exists only while the count is above zero, which is proved in Lean, and here it's pressed through the accessibility tree.
